summary: A cave bat that spends the whole year underground, with most of its kind wintering in a handful of caves.
description: A medium-sized bat about 3.5 inches long, with a wingspan of 10 to 11 inches.  Its fur is gray, and often fades to reddish-brown by early summer.
habitat: Caves, all year, in limestone country.  Summer colonies sometimes use dams, mines, culverts, and the undersides of bridges.  It feeds over open water.
life: Gray bats roost on cave ceilings and are easily disturbed.  About 95 percent of them hibernate in nine caves, which leaves the species exposed to a single bad event.
alabama: Found across the state except the southwest quarter.  It is common near the Tennessee River in north Alabama, with smaller numbers in the central and southern parts.  Fern Cave, in north Alabama, is one of the nine great wintering caves.
countiesText: Statewide except the southwest; most common in the Tennessee Valley
range: The southeastern and midwestern United States
threats: Disturbance of roosting bats by people, vandalism, the sealing or poor gating of caves, pesticides, and floods.  Wind turbines and a changing climate are newer concerns.
notes: Most of the major wintering caves are now permanently protected.

summary: A small bat that winters packed together in a few cold caves and summers under the loose bark of trees.
description: A medium-sized bat much like the common little brown bat, with dull grayish-chestnut fur, pinkish-cinnamon underparts, and small, delicate hind feet.
habitat: It winters in cool caves and abandoned mines where the temperature holds steady.  In summer it roosts under the peeling bark of large trees, often dead ones, in forest.
life: Indiana bats hibernate in tight clusters on cave ceilings.  Females gather in maternity colonies and usually raise one pup a year.
alabama: Found only in the northern third of the state.  Nine cave systems have records, though some may rest on misidentified bats.  Sauta Cave held the largest wintering group, about 250 bats from 1992 to 2002, and Bankhead National Forest holds two more sites.  No maternity colony is known in Alabama.
countiesText: The northern third of the state
range: The eastern half of the United States; most winter at a few sites in Missouri, Indiana, and Illinois
threats: Disturbance of hibernating bats, the commercial use of caves, loss of summer roost trees, pesticides, and white-nose syndrome, a fungal disease.  The population has roughly halved since it was listed.

summary: A long-eared forest bat that white-nose syndrome has all but emptied from its wintering caves.
description: A small bat, 3 to 3.7 inches long, with a brown back, a paler belly, and notably long ears.
habitat: It winters in cold, humid caves and mines where the air is still.  In the warm months it roosts under bark and in tree cavities, mostly in forest.
life: Females gather in maternity colonies, often of 30 to 60 bats, and each bears one pup.
alabama: Its range in the state is poorly known.  Small numbers have been recorded in the Bear Creek system and Bankhead National Forest in the northwest, and it likely lives in other forested uplands across north Alabama.  The state has also reported a breeding population on the coast.
countiesText: Northwest Alabama, and probably other northern uplands; also reported on the coast
range: Parts of 37 states, the District of Columbia, and eight Canadian provinces
threats: White-nose syndrome above all: counts at affected wintering sites have fallen by 97 to 100 percent.  Wind turbines, loss of summer habitat, and disturbance in winter add to it.
notes: Listed as threatened in 2015, and reclassified as endangered by a rule published November 30, 2022 (87 FR 73488).

summary: One of the smallest bats in North America, once common across Alabama and now proposed for listing as endangered.
description: About 3 to 3.5 inches long.  Each hair is dark at the base, pale in the middle, and dark at the tip.  The coat often looks yellowish, but can be gray, brown, or black.
habitat: From spring to fall it roosts among the leaves of hardwood trees.  In winter it hibernates in caves and mines, and in the South also in culverts and trees.
life: It usually roosts alone, and feeds on small insects over water and along forest edges.  Females usually bear two young.
alabama: Found statewide, and long counted among the most common bats in Alabama.  In winter almost any sizable cave is likely to hold some.  In the south of the state it may feed all year in warm weather.
range: The eastern and central United States, southern Canada, Mexico, and Central America
threats: White-nose syndrome has cut winter colonies by 90 to 100 percent at affected sites.
notes: The Service proposed listing the bat as endangered in September 2022.  It has no row on the federal list as of the date this site was checked.

seasonNote: They reach the northern Gulf coast around early April and leave for Florida by October
summary: A large, slow, plant-eating mammal that summers in Alabama's coastal waters and winters in Florida.
description: A large aquatic mammal that never leaves the water.  It grazes on seagrass and other water plants, and favors shallow grass beds near deeper channels.
habitat: Warm, shallow coastal waters, bays, and rivers with seagrass and a source of fresh water.  In winter it must find warm water, such as springs and the outflows of power plants, because long exposure to cold can kill it.
alabama: A warm-season visitor.  Manatees arrive on the northern Gulf coast around early April, as the water warms, and return to Florida by October.  The Dauphin Island Sea Lab has tagged and tracked manatees in Alabama waters since 2009, and collects sightings from the public.
range: Florida and Puerto Rico in the United States, with summer wanderers along the Gulf and Atlantic coasts
threats: Collisions with boats, which are the leading cause of death from human activity, and the loss of warm-water refuges in winter.  If you see one, slow down, cut the motor, and stay at least 100 feet away.
notes: Listed as endangered in 1967, and reclassified as threatened by a rule published April 5, 2017 (82 FR 16668).

summary: A small, pale mouse found only in the dunes of the Baldwin County coast.
description: A small, pale mouse of the dunes.  Its light coat is an inherited trait.
habitat: Coastal dunes: the frontal dunes, and the higher scrub dunes behind them, which give refuge when storms wash over the beach.
life: It is active at night and eats seeds, fruit, and insects.  It breeds all year, most in winter, and an average mouse lives about nine months.
alabama: Found only in Baldwin County, on the Fort Morgan Peninsula and in Gulf Shores and Orange Beach, including the Perdue Unit of Bon Secour National Wildlife Refuge.  The Service's review put its range at about 2,450 acres along some 13 miles of coast.
threats: Loss of dunes to building, hurricanes, feral cats, artificial lighting, and a rising sea.  The mouse recovered slowly from the hurricanes of 2004 and 2005, and its numbers swing widely.

summary: A beach mouse confined to Perdido Key, the barrier island that Alabama shares with Florida.
description: A small mouse with large ears and protruding eyes.  The head and body are about 3 inches long and the tail about 2.  It is grayish fawn to wood brown above and white below, with the white reaching up to the eyes and ears.
habitat: Frontal dunes covered in sea oats, and the scrub dunes behind them.  The two need to stay connected.
life: It is active at night, and lives mostly on the seeds of sea oats and beach grass.  When seeds run short, in late winter and early spring, it turns to insects and the fruit of sea rocket.
alabama: Perdido Key spans the state line.  Critical habitat for the mouse includes a unit at Gulf State Park, along with Perdido Key State Park, Gulf Islands National Seashore, and private land on the Florida side.
range: Perdido Key, in Alabama and Florida
threats: Loss of dunes to building, feral cats, artificial lighting, and trash that draws predators and competitors.  Moving mice between sites is credited with saving the population in the 1980s.
notes: Critical habitat was revised by a rule published October 12, 2006 (71 FR 60238).

summary: A wolf of the Southeast, gone from Alabama since the 1920s and now wild in only one place.
description: A wolf between the coyote and the gray wolf in size.  It is mostly brown and buff, with black along the back and reddish fur behind the ears and on the neck and legs.
habitat: It once used country of many kinds across the Southeast.  The one wild population today lives in eastern North Carolina.
alabama: Red wolves once lived across Alabama.  By 1921 they were reported nearly gone, holding on last in the rough hill country from Walker County northwest to Colbert County, and they vanished from the state in the early 1920s.
range: One wild population, in eastern North Carolina
threats: Gunshots and vehicle strikes, and interbreeding with coyotes, which grows worse as the wolves grow fewer.  The red wolf was declared extinct in the wild in 1980, and a few dozen now live wild in North Carolina.

summary: The big cat of the Southeast, probably the cougar that once ranged over Alabama, and gone from the state since the 1800s.
description: A large, long-tailed cat, pale brown or rusty above and whitish or buff below, with dark marks on the tail tip, the backs of the ears, and the sides of the nose.  Males weigh about 100 to 150 pounds and measure nearly 7 feet from nose to tail tip.  Females are smaller.
habitat: In Alabama, cougars kept to remote uplands, rough country, and bottomland swamps.
alabama: Cougars once lived across Alabama, and the Florida panther was probably the kind found over much of the state.  They likely disappeared around the middle of the 1800s.  Sightings reported today usually prove to be bobcats, coyotes, house pets, or escaped captives.
threats: The profile read for this entry does not list threats.  The recovery plan covers them.
